title: Ararat
full_review:
"Ararat" (Miramax) is a powerful tale of a contemporary Armenian family's journey from dysfunction to healing, as family members come to grips with the ghosts of their collective cultural past -- the genocidal extermination of Armenians by Ottoman Turkish forces in 1915.

Acclaimed Canadian writer-director Atom Egoyan masterfully weaves past and present, subtly fashioning a tapestry of the human condition, as well as a provocative indictment of man's capacity for cruelty. Divergent storylines blend seamlessly in this compelling exploration of the nature of truth, and the repercussions of denial on both a grand and an intimate scale.

Raffi (newcomer David Alpay), an idealistic young Armenian living in Toronto with his estranged mother, Ani (Arsinee Khanjian), cannot escape the shadow of the death of his Armenian nationalist father, killed while attempting to assassinate a Turkish official. Raffi's romantic involvement with his disaffected stepsister, Cecilia (Marie-Josee Croze), has created an emotional rift between him and Ani. Ani, an art historian at the university, finds solace in her near-religious obsession with a painting, "The Artist and His Mother," by Arshile Gorky (1904-1948), an Armenian considered by many as one of the pioneers of abstract expressionism.

Before emigrating to America, Gorky survived the Armenian genocide, which resulted in the extermination of two-thirds of the Armenian population, a crime still denied by the Turkish government (Hitler himself quelled his officers' hesitancy to proceed with their 'final solution' by asking, "Does anyone even remember the Armenian genocide?"). Ani's knowledge of Gorky's life and work lands her a position as a consultant on a film about the tragic events of 1915 by legendary (but fictitious) director Edward Saroyan (Charles Aznavour), who lost his own mother in the massacre.

This "film-within-a-film," based on the historical eyewitness account written by an American missionary, is the nexus used by Egoyan to link past and present. Forced to confront the painful legacy of these atrocities, Ani and Raffi find the resolve to exorcise the personal demons that have tormented their relationship.

While capturing the barbarity inflicted on the Armenian people with disturbingly graphic effectiveness, the film fails to plumb the profundity of the enigma of evil. Egoyan seems content to hold a mirror up to man's darker nature rather than offer any illumination of the mystery of suffering, though in the face of such unspeakable horror any exegesis admittedly would be woefully inadequate.

Religious references and iconography permeate much of the film, yet the divine element of the mystery of suffering is noticeably absent. Several characters pose the eternal existential question "why?" but the filmmaker embraces a somewhat humanistic view, lowering their gaze from the heavens to each other. Egoyan's choices suggest that we must find or make our own answers by sheer acts of will or creativity when confronted with such senseless evil, and not search for any transcendent or redemptive value in suffering.

Though several sequences are difficult to watch, Egoyan, who is himself of Armenian descent, deserves credit for bringing attention to a dark -- and, unfortunately, neglected -- chapter of 20th-century history and for reminding us that "what is destroyed in genocide are not only human lives, but the very imprint of humanity in us."

Due to explicit violence, depictions of torture and a rape, a sexual encounter, nudity, sporadic profanity and some rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
